concepts.decision: Use when algorithms, libraries, protocols, certificates, or trust anchors may need replacement.
concepts.definition: Ability to inventory, change, test, and retire cryptographic dependencies under control.
concepts.failureExample: A hard-coded algorithm in a device cannot be changed when policy deprecates it.
concepts.label: Cryptographic Agility

concepts.decision: Match the role, data lifetime, threat, performance, interoperability, and authoritative policy.
concepts.definition: Choosing approved algorithms and parameters for a defined protection role.
concepts.failureExample: A vendor calls one algorithm “quantum safe” without naming its protocol function.
concepts.label: Algorithm Selection

concepts.decision: Build it before prioritizing or scheduling a migration.
concepts.definition: Record of cryptographic uses, implementations, keys, certificates, owners, and dependencies.
concepts.failureExample: An embedded library and its certificate chain are invisible until an emergency replacement.
concepts.label: Cryptographic Inventory

concepts.decision: Prioritize by public-key dependency, data lifetime, exposure, support, and migration feasibility.
concepts.definition: Cryptographic approaches intended to address quantum-era threats to relevant public-key uses.
concepts.failureExample: A team replaces every symmetric control immediately without identifying the actual public-key risk.
concepts.label: Post Quantum Cryptography

concepts.decision: Use only where its physical deployment, endpoint, lifecycle, and trust assumptions fit the requirement.
concepts.definition: Specialized physical key-establishment approach with operational and integration assumptions.
concepts.failureExample: A proposal treats QKD as a substitute for identity, endpoint security, and authorization.
concepts.label: Quantum Key Distribution

concepts.decision: Require approved profile, compatibility test, authority, rollout evidence, rollback, and deprecation date.
concepts.definition: Controlled transition from one cryptographic profile or dependency to another.
concepts.failureExample: A rollout silently falls back to a deprecated weak protocol when a partner fails.
concepts.label: Migration

concepts.decision: Test protocols, certificates, hardware, services, and external partners before broad rollout.
concepts.definition: Ability of implementations and partners to exchange and validate cryptographic operations correctly.
concepts.failureExample: A new certificate profile prevents a critical partner from authenticating.
concepts.label: Interoperability

concepts.decision: Address long-lived sensitive data and exposed dependencies before lower-consequence uses.
concepts.definition: Ordering migration work by consequence, exposure, confidentiality or verification lifetime, and feasibility.
concepts.failureExample: A team migrates easy internal tools while a long-retention external service stays unassessed.
concepts.label: Risk Prioritization

concepts.decision: Use an approved mechanism that fits peer authentication, protocol, and lifecycle requirements.
concepts.definition: Protocol process by which parties obtain a shared secret or authenticated keying material.
concepts.failureExample: A key-establishment mechanism is used as though it also signs software releases.
concepts.label: Key Establishment

concepts.decision: Use only for its key-establishment role within an approved, tested protocol profile.
concepts.definition: NIST FIPS 203 standardized ML-KEM for post-quantum key establishment.
concepts.failureExample: A supplier claims ML-KEM signs releases or secures every protocol layer.
concepts.label: Ml Kem

concepts.decision: Use when the required role is signing with compatible implementation, certificate, and verifier support.
concepts.definition: NIST FIPS 204 standardized ML-DSA as a post-quantum digital-signature algorithm.
concepts.failureExample: A migration replaces a key-establishment mechanism with ML-DSA without redesigning the protocol role.
concepts.label: Ml Dsa

concepts.decision: Select only through approved profiles and testing of its signature, performance, and interoperability role.
concepts.definition: NIST FIPS 205 standardized SLH-DSA as a post-quantum digital-signature algorithm.
concepts.failureExample: A team assumes ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are interchangeable without a policy or compatibility decision.
concepts.label: Slh Dsa

concepts.decision: Assign when an inventory entry must remain current through change and deprecation.
concepts.definition: Accountable role that maintains the mapping from cryptographic use to system, dependency, data, and lifecycle.
concepts.failureExample: A migration list names algorithms but nobody owns embedded library discovery.
concepts.label: Crypto Inventory Owner

concepts.decision: Assign before pilot and production changes so fallback cannot silently reinstate deprecated protection.
concepts.definition: Role authorized to approve profiles, exceptions, rollout, rollback, and retirement in a cryptographic transition.
concepts.failureExample: An emergency rollback restores a weak protocol with no expiry or approval.
concepts.label: Migration Change Authority

misconceptions.claim: Quantum key distribution eliminates the need for certificates, endpoints, and key management.
misconceptions.correction: It addresses a narrow key-establishment context and still relies on authenticated operational, endpoint, and lifecycle controls.

misconceptions.claim: ML-KEM alone makes a protocol quantum safe.
misconceptions.correction: A protected protocol still needs appropriate authentication/signatures, implementation assurance, endpoint and key management, and an interoperable lifecycle.

outcome: Plan justified cryptographic migration and evaluate quantum-related claims by inventorying dependencies, prioritizing exposure, and validating a controlled transition.

sections.body: Agility begins with an inventory of algorithms, libraries, protocols, certificates, keys, owners, data classifications, interoperability partners, hardware or service dependencies, and expiry dates. Abstracting every detail is not required, but untracked embedded choices make migration difficult. Define approved cryptographic profiles, procurement requirements, change authority, test environments, compatibility plans, telemetry, rollback criteria, and deprecation dates. Treat a change in algorithm, parameter, library, or trust anchor as a controlled architecture and operations change.
keyPoints: You cannot prioritize migration reliably without knowing where cryptography is used and what data it protects.
Agility is governance, engineering, testing, and operations—not only modular code.
sections.title: Build the conditions for controlled change

sections.body: The outline includes quantum among cryptographic methods and quantum key distribution in the PKI context. Quantum computing risk discussions commonly focus on whether certain public-key approaches may face different future feasibility assumptions; the appropriate response depends on data sensitivity and required confidentiality lifetime, not a claim that every system is already broken. Quantum key distribution is a specialized key-establishment approach with physical, operational, integration, and trust assumptions; it is not a universal replacement for PKI, endpoint security, authorization, or key lifecycle management.
keyPoints: Long-lived sensitive data can justify earlier planning even when migration is not immediate.
Quantum-related technology still needs identity, operations, availability, and endpoint controls.
sections.title: Separate quantum concepts from unsupported certainty

sections.body: Rank uses by data longevity, impact, external exposure, migration complexity, supplier support, and assurance evidence. Pilot approved replacement profiles where compatible, test performance and failure behavior, validate certificate and key processes, coordinate partners, and retain a time-bounded rollback plan that does not silently restore a deprecated weak state. Record exceptions with owners and expiration. The successful outcome is verified maintained protection during transition, not merely a list of new algorithm names.
keyPoints: Migration must include partners, devices, libraries, trust anchors, and recovery procedures.
A fallback can be necessary, but it must be constrained and removed deliberately.
sections.title: Prioritize and validate a transition

sections.body: NIST finalized FIPS 203 ML-KEM for key establishment in 2024; related final signature standards are FIPS 204 ML-DSA and FIPS 205 SLH-DSA. A standard’s existence does not prove every protocol, partner, device, certificate workflow, or implementation is ready to migrate. Inventory public-key uses and confidentiality/verification lifetime, identify approved profiles and interoperability constraints, then test a governed transition. The failure mode is buying a “quantum-safe” claim without knowing the protocol role, cryptographic boundary, implementation assurance, fallback, or partner support.
keyPoints: ML-KEM establishes a shared secret; it is not a label for every cryptographic function.
Migration priority follows data lifetime, exposure, dependency, and safe deployability.
